questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Federalism as a division of sovereignty
questions.learningObjective: name the arrangement in which national and state governments share sovereign authority
questions.stem: A lawyer describes the national system by saying that two governments each draw their authority from its own constitution and each may make law binding on the same people. Which term names that arrangement?

options.text: Federalism, in which sovereign authority is divided between distinct national and state governments
Confederalism, in which the national government holds all sovereign power and the states hold none
options.misconception: believes central authority is complete in a confederal arrangement

options.text: Unitarism, in which a single central legislature holds every power of government in the country
options.misconception: believes a unitary system concentrates all authority in one legislature

options.text: Supremacy, in which one level of government is declared the highest law of the land
options.misconception: confuses the arrangement of governments with the rule for conflicts

questions.explanation: Federalism is the division of sovereignty between a national government and state governments, each created by its own constitution and each with lawmaking authority within its own sphere. Confederalism instead leaves final authority with the states and makes the central body dependent on them, unitarism concentrates authority in a single centre, and supremacy is the rule that resolves conflicts between the levels rather than a name for the arrangement itself.
questions.hint: Ask which level holds the final authority, and whether it needs the other's permission to act.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Ambiguity of an enumerated list with a reservation
questions.learningObjective: explain the difficulty a broad list of powers creates beside a clause reserving the rest
questions.stem: A constitution lists the national government's powers in broad terms and reserves everything not delegated to the states, yet defines few of the broad terms. What difficulty does that pairing create for a court?

options.text: The court must fit a claimed power inside a broad entry, and the list answers few of the questions that fit raises
The court must first find whether a state delegated the power to the nation before the nation may use it
options.misconception: believes a state transfers powers to the national government

options.text: The court must decide whether later state practice has repealed one of the broad constitutional entries
options.misconception: believes state practice can repeal a constitutional power

options.text: The court must treat every power not listed in express terms as reserved to the nation instead
options.misconception: believes unenumerated powers belong to the national government

questions.explanation: The difficulty is the ambiguity created by pairing a list of broadly worded powers with a clause reserving all the rest, so a court must fit a claimed power inside one of the broad entries while the list itself defines few of them. A state does not delegate powers to the nation, later state practice cannot repeal a constitutional entry, and unenumerated powers are reserved to the states and the people rather than to the national government.
questions.hint: Ask what a court has to do with a claim that sounds broader than any entry the list names.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Implied powers and incidental authority
questions.learningObjective: state what a party must establish to support a power the constitution does not name
questions.stem: A lawyer argues that a national statute is valid because it carries out a purpose the constitution states, even though no clause names the statute's subject. What must the lawyer establish for the argument to succeed?

options.text: That a power granted to the nation covers the subject, and that the statute is appropriate to executing it
That no state ever passed a law on the same subject before the statute was enacted
options.misconception: believes earlier state silence supplies a constitutional basis

options.text: That the purpose appears among the objectives recited in the preamble to the constitution
options.misconception: believes a preamble objective can support a power not granted

options.text: That the statute was duly enacted by both chambers and signed before the argument was made
options.misconception: confuses the ordinary process of enactment with the source of the power

questions.explanation: This is the argument from implied powers, which runs through the Necessary and Proper Clause: the claim is that the constitution granted a power and the statute is appropriate to carrying that power into execution, so the statute must be judged by its relation to an enumerated power. Earlier state silence, an objective recited in the preamble, and the ordinary process of enactment do not supply the constitutional basis, because the difficulty is the absence of a granted power rather than a defect in how a bill was passed.
questions.hint: Ask which granted power the statute is said to be executing, and how it is connected to it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Concurrent power and a national floor
questions.learningObjective: state the effect of concurrent legislation where the two levels are consistent
questions.stem: A national statute sets a minimum safety standard for a workplace, and a state then enacts a stricter rule that meets the minimum and adds requirements of its own. Is the state rule valid?

options.text: Yes, because concurrent legislation may add to a national floor where the two rules are consistent
No, because a national statute occupies the whole of its subject and bars all state regulation
options.misconception: believes a national statute always displaces state law on the same subject

options.text: No, because only the national legislature may regulate the subject of workplace safety
options.misconception: believes safety regulation is reserved to the national level alone

options.text: Yes, but only where the state first secures the consent of the national legislature
options.misconception: believes a state needs legislative consent to add to national law

questions.explanation: Where the same power is held by both levels, national law sets a floor that a state may build upon, and a stricter state rule consistent with that minimum remains valid. That is the difference between concurrent powers, where both may act, and an exclusive national power, where a national statute displaces state regulation because the constitution granted the subject to the nation alone. No legislative consent is needed, because the state is exercising a power it already holds rather than borrowing one.
questions.hint: Ask whether a state that does more than the nation is stepping outside its own power.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Scope of the commerce power
questions.learningObjective: explain why the commerce power reaches more than the words about interstate trade suggest
questions.stem: The commerce power is worded as authority to regulate commerce with foreign nations and among the several states, yet the conduct it reaches has come to include a great deal of local activity. How is that possible?

options.text: The power is not confined to a few listed subjects but reaches activity that substantially affects commerce
The clause was amended so that the words about foreign nations and the states no longer limit it
options.misconception: believes the commerce power was rewritten to remove its limits

options.text: The power is really a police power that belongs to the states and is borrowed by the nation
options.misconception: believes the nation exercises a state police power by permission

options.text: The power reaches any conduct at all once the nation has legislated once on a subject
options.misconception: believes one statute on a subject swallows the whole field

questions.explanation: The commerce power is a grant of authority to regulate commerce rather than a list of the subjects commerce touches, so a court asks whether the activity is commerce among the states or substantially affects such commerce, which reaches a great deal of local activity. The clause has not been amended to strip away its words, it is not a state police power the nation borrows, and its reach is bounded, because even a substantial effect has to be tied to commerce rather than to any conduct whatever.
questions.hint: Ask whether the power names subjects or names a regulatory relationship.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Taxing and spending as separate authorities
questions.learningObjective: state what follows from the tax power and the spending power being granted separately
questions.stem: The constitution grants the national government one power to raise money and a second power to spend money, in different words and in different clauses. What follows from that separation?

options.text: Either may be exercised on its own, and spending does not require that revenue be raised by taxation
Spending always requires revenue to have been raised first, so the two must be used in that order
options.misconception: believes the spending power depends on using the taxing power first

options.text: Taxing always requires that the money be spent, because revenue raised for no purpose is unlawful
options.misconception: believes revenue must be earmarked for a programme when raised

options.text: Only the taxing power is limited by the constitution, and spending may be directed as the nation sees fit
options.misconception: believes the constitution constrains taxing but leaves spending unbounded

questions.explanation: The power to lay and collect taxes and the power to spend are distinct grants, and money may be spent out of receipts on duties as readily as out of income taxes, so a spending measure does not need a revenue act behind it. Nor does a tax have to be tied to a particular programme, and while both powers are constrained by the constitution, holding that only taxation is limited discards the limits that apply to the purposes for which money may be spent.
questions.hint: Ask whether one of the two authorities depends on the other having been exercised.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Regulating individuals against commanding a state
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a rule binding individuals from an order directed to a state
questions.stem: Congress wants waste collection to meet a national standard, and considers two routes: a rule binding every household in a state, or an order telling the state itself to build facilities. Which statement describes the difference?

options.text: A rule binding individuals directly is generally permissible, while an order to a state is not
Both routes are permissible, so the choice of instrument makes no constitutional difference at all
options.misconception: believes the instrument makes no difference to a state's legal position

options.text: Only a rule binding individuals is impermissible, because it reaches into the workings of a state
options.misconception: believes a direct rule on individuals is what commandeers a state

options.text: Neither route is permissible, because waste collection is reserved entirely to the states
options.misconception: believes the subject matter alone makes both routes unavailable

questions.explanation: The distinction runs between regulating the people of a state and commanding the state. A national rule that applies to households, firms and other private actors regulates individuals and is generally within the national government's reach, whereas an order directing a state to build or operate something is the commandeering the anti-commandeering principle forbids. Neither route is barred because the subject is reserved, since the objection concerns which actor the command runs to rather than the subject of the demand.
questions.hint: Ask whether the rule reaches the people of a state or the government of that state.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Express preemption
questions.learningObjective: identify preemption that operates through the words of a federal statute
questions.stem: A federal statute states in terms that no state or local rule on the licensing of a particular trade is valid. Which kind of preemption do those words accomplish?

options.text: Express preemption, in which the statute itself closes the field to state and local rules
Field preemption, in which a federal scheme is so complete that it leaves no room at all
options.misconception: confuses express preemption with field preemption

options.text: Conflict preemption, in which a state rule is invalid because it clashes with federal law
options.misconception: confuses express preemption with conflict preemption

options.text: No preemption, in which a state licensing scheme survives any federal wording on the subject
options.misconception: believes express words in a statute cannot displace state law

questions.explanation: The clause described is express preemption, which works through the statute's own words declaring that the field is closed to other bodies, so the court has only to apply what the legislature said. Field preemption is inferred from a scheme so thorough that no room is left, and conflict preemption is inferred from two rules that cannot both be obeyed, so where a legislature has spoken directly no inference is required.
questions.hint: Ask whether the legislature said so in words, or whether the court has to infer it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Field preemption
questions.learningObjective: identify preemption inferred from the comprehensiveness of a federal scheme
questions.stem: A national licensing scheme covers registration, renewal, fees, appeals and enforcement in detail, and it says nothing about state licensing. A state licensing board asks whether its own scheme survives. What is the likely answer?

options.text: The national scheme occupies the field, so the state scheme is displaced even without express words
The state scheme survives, because preemption always requires an express statement of intent
options.misconception: believes preemption can never be inferred from the scheme itself

options.text: Both schemes operate, because field preemption applies only to matters of criminal law
options.misconception: believes field preemption is confined to criminal law

options.text: The state scheme survives, because a national scheme can never occupy a field on its own
options.misconception: believes a comprehensive national scheme leaves room for a state scheme

questions.explanation: Field preemption is inferred where the national scheme is so thorough in addressing a subject that a state scheme would contradict or undo what the legislature settled, and the absence of words is exactly what makes the inference necessary. It does not depend on an express statement, it is not confined to any branch of substantive law, and the setting of a licensing scheme that comprehensively addresses registration, renewal, fees, appeals and enforcement is where the doctrine is at its clearest.
questions.hint: Ask how much of the subject the national scheme has already settled.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Conflict preemption
questions.learningObjective: identify preemption arising from two rules that cannot both be obeyed
questions.stem: A federal statute requires one label on a product and a state statute requires a different and additional label on the same product, so obeying both is impossible. What is the name for the outcome?

options.text: Conflict preemption, in which obeying the state rule would make compliance with the federal rule impossible
Express preemption, in which a federal statute voids a conflicting state rule in terms
options.misconception: confuses conflict preemption with express preemption

options.text: Field preemption, in which a comprehensive scheme leaves no room for the state rule
options.misconception: confuses conflict preemption with field preemption

options.text: Supremacy, in which a court must choose between two rules of equal legal authority
options.misconception: confuses the conflict rule with the general rule of priority

questions.explanation: Conflict preemption is the third route, and it turns on impossibility or on the danger of frustrating the national purpose, which is what occurs when obeying the state label makes compliance with the federal label unavailable. Express preemption needs words in the statute, field preemption needs a comprehensive scheme, and supremacy is the general principle that valid federal law prevails rather than a separate mechanism with its own test.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two requirements can be satisfied at the same time.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The proviso on the spending power
questions.learningObjective: state the limit the reserved-powers clause places on the spending power
questions.stem: The clause reserving powers to the states ends with words about the spending power and a limit on it. Which limit does that proviso impose?

options.text: That the national government may not compel a state to provide the rest of a programme's cost
That the national government may not spend on any purpose a state legislature has objected to
options.misconception: believes a state's written protest defeats federal spending

options.text: That the national government may not offer a grant unless every state receives one as well
options.misconception: believes a grant must be offered to every state on equal terms

options.text: That the national government may not attach any condition to federal money, however the statute words it
options.misconception: believes the proviso strips the spending power of all conditions

questions.explanation: The proviso provides that the national government may not compel a state to accede to the sufficiency of federal money for a programme it must carry on, and that is a limit written into the clause itself rather than one supplied by a later court. A state may protest or decline, so a protest is not a veto, equal treatment of the states is not required, and the proviso does not strip the spending power of its power to attach conditions at all.
questions.hint: Ask what the clause forbids the national government to force a state to supply.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Compelling state officers to administer a programme
questions.learningObjective: apply the anti-commandeering principle to a requirement aimed at state officers
questions.stem: A federal official tells a governor that federal law requires the state to administer a federal benefit programme through state offices, and adds that nothing will be taken away for complying. Why is the instruction defective?

options.text: Congress may not require a state to administer a federal programme through its own officers
Congress may not pay a state for work its officers would otherwise have had to perform
options.misconception: believes paying a state for administrative work is itself the defect

options.text: Congress may not create a benefit programme whose eligibility rules differ among the states
options.misconception: believes variation in eligibility rules is what the principle forbids

options.text: Congress may not require a state to keep records of the work its officers carry out
options.misconception: believes a records requirement on a state is a prohibited command

questions.explanation: The anti-commandeering principle forbids the national government to require a state to administer a federal programme through its own officers, whether or not money is attached, because the state is being made the instrument of a federal programme rather than a participant in it. Conditions on federal money, records requirements, and differences in eligibility among the states are all permissible, so the defect lies in the compulsion of state officers and not in any of those features.
questions.hint: Ask who is being made to carry out the programme, and whether anyone can decline the job.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Purpose and period limits on appropriations
questions.learningObjective: state the limits an appropriation places on the use of money
questions.stem: Money has been appropriated for one programme for the current year, and an official wants to move part of it to a different programme that has not been funded this year. What governs that move?

options.text: The law that made the appropriation, which ties the money to its stated purpose and period
The official's own judgement, since an appropriation is simply a pool of available funds
options.misconception: believes appropriated money is a general pool for the agency

options.text: The agency's enabling statute alone, since the appropriation only fixes the total amount
options.misconception: believes the enabling statute governs how appropriated money may be used

options.text: Nothing, provided the total amount the agency spends this year stays the same figure
options.misconception: believes holding the total constant permits any change of purpose

questions.explanation: An appropriation is limited to the purpose and the period the law states, so money cannot be moved to a different programme or used after the period without a law that allows it, which is the rule the purpose statute enforces. The enabling statute defines what the agency may do rather than how much it may spend this year, an appropriation is not a general pool, and keeping the total unchanged does not cure a change in what the money was for.
questions.hint: Ask which law says what the money is for and how long it is available.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: An unfunded federal requirement on a state
questions.learningObjective: describe a federal requirement on a state that carries no federal payment
questions.stem: A federal statute requires every state to operate a benefits office with specified opening hours and staffing, and the federal government contributes no money toward it. Which statement describes the requirement?

options.text: It is a mandate on the state, which must staff and pay for the office from its own resources
It is a grant to the state, since the state is being asked to perform a public function
options.misconception: believes an unfunded federal order is a grant to the state

options.text: It is unenforceable, because the federal government may never direct a state to act at all
options.misconception: believes the federal government may not issue any requirement to a state

options.text: It is invalid, because the constitution requires a federal payment for every state function
options.misconception: believes the constitution mandates federal funding for any state duty

questions.explanation: A federal requirement on a state that carries no federal payment is a mandate, and the state must meet it from its own resources because the money it implies is the state's to find. The absence of a federal payment is an objection about cost rather than about authority, and the order does not become a grant merely because a public function is involved, while a state may always decline federal money whose conditions it dislikes.
questions.hint: Ask whether the state receives anything in return for the work it must perform.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The two budget years
questions.learningObjective: explain why the budget covers a year that has not yet begun
questions.stem: The national budget covers the year that is beginning and the year after it, though money for the second year is not provided until later. What is the point of budgeting a year that has not started?

options.text: The legislature can weigh the second year against the first before commitments in the first year
The executive is free to spend the second year's money during the first year as it sees fit
options.misconception: believes the later year's figures authorise early spending

options.text: The second year receives a fixed level that no later law may change at any point
options.misconception: believes the second year is locked once the budget is adopted

options.text: Each agency may plan two years ahead without any legislative review of the second year
options.misconception: believes the second year bypasses legislative consideration

questions.explanation: Budgeting the second year in advance gives the legislature the chance to see both years together and to make the trade-offs between them explicitly, because commitments made during the first year often run into the second. It does not let an executive spend the second year's money early, it does not freeze the second year, which later legislation may change, and the second-year figures are a plan rather than an entitlement that agencies may draw on.
questions.hint: Ask what the legislature can do with both years at once that it could not do with one.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Authorisation and appropriation
questions.learningObjective: distinguish an authorisation from an appropriation
questions.stem: The legislature enacts a statute creating a programme, and later decides how much money to provide for the current year. Which term names that second step, and what does it do?

options.text: An appropriation, which makes money available for obligation during the year it covers
An authorisation, which makes money available for obligation during the year it covers
options.misconception: attaches the effect of an appropriation to an authorisation

options.text: An appropriation, which tells the agency in detail how the money must be spent
options.misconception: attributes detailed spending directions to an appropriation

options.text: A budget resolution, which makes money available for obligation during the year it covers
options.misconception: attributes the effect of an appropriation to a budget resolution

questions.explanation: An appropriation is the act that makes funds available for obligation, and it fixes the amount available and the period of availability, while an authorisation creates or continues a programme without supplying money. An appropriation states how much may be spent rather than directing the agency how to spend it, and a budget resolution is a framework for later decisions rather than a source of funds available for obligation.
questions.hint: Ask which step actually sets aside money for use this year.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Continuing resolution
questions.learningObjective: state what a continuing resolution does while appropriations are unfinished
questions.stem: The legislature has not finished the appropriations legislation, and programmes must keep running in the meantime. What instrument keeps the money flowing?

options.text: A continuing resolution, which continues funding at the prior rate until a law replaces it
An authorisation, which supplies money until the appropriation is finally enacted
options.misconception: believes an authorisation keeps money flowing during a delay

options.text: A budget resolution, which provides the funds at the level the resolution specifies
options.misconception: believes a budget resolution makes funds available for obligation

options.text: A deferral, which lets an agency pay this year's bills out of next year's funds
options.misconception: believes a deferral is a lawful way to meet obligations during a delay

questions.explanation: A continuing resolution is a statute that continues current funding, commonly at the rate in force for the preceding period and sometimes with special adjustments, so that an agency may keep operating while the appropriations process finishes. An authorisation supplies no money, a budget resolution is a framework rather than an available sum, and deferral is not a device for meeting obligations while the budget is unfinished.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to last year's funding level while the new one is still being written.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The limit on impoundment
questions.learningObjective: identify the statute that limits withholding of appropriated funds
questions.stem: A department official withholds money the legislature has already appropriated, on the ground that the department can manage without it, and says the executive may do so until a law says otherwise. Which principle answers the claim?

options.text: The statutory limit on impoundment, which bars withholding appropriated funds except as a law allows
The executive's inherent authority to manage the budget, which no statute may narrow
options.misconception: believes executive management authority is beyond legislative control

options.text: The appropriations power, which lets each branch decide how to use money once granted
options.misconception: believes each branch controls the money granted to it

options.text: The veto power, which lets the executive refuse to spend until the legislature releases the funds
options.misconception: confuses a refusal to spend with a refusal to sign a bill

questions.explanation: The Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974 limited impoundment by requiring the executive to use rescissions and deferrals through the legislative process rather than withholding appropriated funds on its own, and the ordinary rule is that appropriated money is available until a law provides otherwise. Inherent management authority does not extend to refusing money the legislature provided, the appropriations power belongs to the legislature, and the veto has nothing to say about funds already appropriated.
questions.hint: Ask what the law says about an executive official delaying money the legislature supplied.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Sequestration
questions.learningObjective: state what an automatic spending reduction mechanism does once its trigger is met
questions.stem: Projected receipts have fallen short of the levels a budget resolution set, and a statute requires automatic reductions in federal spending. Which statement describes what that mechanism then does?

options.text: It reduces spending by about the same proportion across the accounts it covers, with no further act
It reduces spending in whichever accounts the executive selects, at the executive's discretion
options.misconception: believes the executive chooses which accounts bear the reduction

options.text: It reduces spending only after both chambers of the legislature have agreed to the cuts
options.misconception: believes the mechanism waits for legislative agreement

options.text: It reduces the interest on the national debt first, and spending only if that is not enough
options.misconception: believes the mechanism operates on debt service before programmes

The executive chooses neither the accounts nor the size of the cut, the mechanism does not depend on legislative agreement once its trigger is met, and it operates on spending rather than on the interest on the debt.
questions.hint: Ask what happens next, given that nobody in the government has to vote.

questions.topic: The unified budget and off-budget items
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose of presenting the budget as a single set of accounts
questions.stem: The national budget presents most receipts and spending in one set of accounts, while a few programmes are shown apart, with their totals excluded from the main figures. What is the point of the unified presentation?

options.text: It shows the whole financial position, so excluded items cannot hide their real cost
It separates discretionary choices from mandatory commitments for the reader's convenience
options.misconception: believes the unified presentation exists to sort programmes by discretion

options.text: It ensures that every agency is financed entirely from the money shown in the main accounts
options.misconception: believes the unified presentation makes off-budget financing disappear

options.text: It separates the accounts of one branch from those of the other two branches
options.misconception: believes the unified presentation is organised by branch

Separate lines within a unified budget are a presentational choice, the presentation cannot make off-budget financing vanish, and no branch has accounts of its own within it.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would fail to see if the totals were not added together.

questions.topic: Deficit against debt
questions.learningObjective: distinguish the deficit for a period from the accumulated national debt
questions.stem: The government spends more than it receives during a year, and the difference is added to what it already owes. Which statement describes the relationship between those two figures?

options.text: The deficit is the gap for that year, and the debt is the total owed across many years
The two are one figure shown in two ways, since each expresses the same yearly shortfall
options.misconception: believes the deficit and the debt are two names for a single number

options.text: The debt is the gap for the current year, and the deficit is the total owed since founding
options.misconception: reverses the period covered by the deficit and by the debt

options.text: A deficit reduces the debt, because spending beyond receipts releases money held by the government
options.misconception: believes overspending shrinks the outstanding obligation

questions.explanation: A deficit is the excess of spending over receipts in a single period, while the debt is the outstanding total owed once many such periods have accumulated, so a deficit year adds to the total and a surplus year subtracts from it. The two are figures for different spans of time rather than two names for one number, and what the government owes is not money it holds, which is why overspending increases rather than reduces the obligation.
questions.hint: Ask which figure covers one year and which one carries every earlier year with it.

questions.topic: Automatic offset of budget changes
questions.learningObjective: state what an automatic offset mechanism does to a proposed budget change
questions.stem: A legislative rule provides that any increase in spending in one account must be matched by an equal reduction elsewhere, and that the matching happens on its own. What is the design of that rule?

options.text: Automatic offset, which holds the net effect on the budget at zero without a new act of Congress
A balanced budget rule, which requires receipts and spending to match within every year

questions.topic: A dispute about an occupied field
questions.learningObjective: identify which route of preemption a described scheme occupies

Express preemption, arising from words in the national statute about local rules
options.misconception: confuses field preemption with express preemption

options.text: Conflict preemption, arising from two requirements that cannot both be obeyed

options.misconception: believes only express statutory words can displace a state law

Only the national statute applies, because valid federal law is always exclusive of state law

options.text: Only the state statute applies, because a state may always regulate its own residents
options.misconception: believes state law always prevails against national law

options.misconception: believes the courts must leave a covered conflict to the political branches

questions.learningObjective: identify what displaces a state rule that cannot coexist with a federal one

The national statute is longer, which is express preemption and the state rule gives way
options.misconception: believes the length of a statute determines preemption

options.text: The state rule is newer, which is field preemption and the state rule gives way
options.misconception: believes recency between two statutes decides preemption

options.text: The state rule is stricter, which is supremacy and the state rule gives way
options.misconception: believes strictness and the general priority rule decide the outcome

options.misconception: names an absolute limit rather than a comparison figure

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How the anti-commandeering principle and the spending power divide
questions.learningObjective: explain how a prohibition on commanding states coexists with a power to condition money
questions.stem: Congress may not order a state to enact a law, yet it may attach conditions to money a state is free to decline. Explain how both statements can be true, and what that arrangement permits in practice.

answer.exemplar: The line between the two powers is compulsion. An order telling a state legislature what law to pass makes the state an instrument of a national programme, and the anti-commandeering principle forbids that because a state in the union is a sovereign, not an office of the federal government. A condition on federal money leaves the choice with the state, because a state that dislikes the condition may keep its own money and run its own programme, while one that finds the national programme useful accepts on the stated terms. In practice the national government can therefore set a floor for how a federally funded activity is carried out and can attach requirements to participation, but it cannot reach a state that declines to participate. The test is whether refusal remains real: while it does, a spending condition is an offer, and once the government frames a condition as something a state must do on pain of a separate legal penalty, it has become a command and the principle bites.

questions.explanation: A strong answer identifies compulsion as the dividing line, states plainly that a state may decline the money, and shows how the same subject yields different results depending on the instrument chosen. An answer that calls a spending condition a disguised command without saying why it is not one, or that omits the possibility of refusal, misses the distinction the question turns on.
questions.hint: Ask what the state can still refuse, and who decides the terms of the offer.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: How a proposal becomes spendable money
questions.learningObjective: trace the steps from a budget proposal to funds that may be obligated
questions.stem: Money does not reach a programme merely because a proposal has been announced. Trace the steps by which a proposal becomes money an agency may actually spend, and name two things that can stop it.

answer.exemplar: A proposal begins as a request, which is neither law nor money. The legislature must authorise the activity by statute, because an agency holds no power the legislature has not given it, and it must appropriate the sum, because the authorisation says what may be done while the appropriation says how much may be spent in a period; a budget resolution frames the totals but supplies neither. Only after an appropriation is money available, and only then may an agency obligate it, and only for the purpose and the period the law states. Two things commonly stop the process. If no appropriation is enacted in time, a continuing resolution keeps the prior funding level alive but supplies nothing new. And if appropriated money is withheld on executive judgment rather than through the process the impoundment statute requires, the spending does not happen even though the money exists.

questions.explanation: A strong answer separates the step that creates authority from the step that supplies money, and names two distinct obstacles with a mechanism for each. An answer that treats a request or a budget resolution as if it made money available, or that stops at authorisation, never reaches the part of the process the question asks about.
questions.hint: Ask what the request lacks, which two legislative steps follow, and where an obstruction can appear.
